tagline: Curving mountain roads connect Christmas tree farms and towns shaped by railroads.
intro: North of Boone, NC 194 becomes narrow and curving beyond Sands, reaching Todd through the High Country. The New River Valley Byway has two sections: NC 194 from Boone to Baldwin, noted for Christmas tree farms, and NC 88 between Jefferson and Laurel Springs. NCDOT includes New River Valley in its scenic-byway guide, describing the state program as an alternative to major highways that introduces travelers to North Carolina's history, geography and culture.

Around 1953, NC 194 extended through Boone and replaced an older US 221 alignment through Todd to Baldwin. It continued along US 221 to West Jefferson. In 1981, the shared US 221/NC 194 route moved to another road between Baldwin and West Jefferson, leaving Beaver Creek School Road behind.

From Boone, follow the sequence through Todd to Baldwin, where NC 194 rejoins US 221 and the road widens. In West Jefferson, NC 194 leaves US 221 and runs downtown with US 221 Business. West Jefferson sits in a valley between Mount Jefferson to the east and Paddy Mountain to the west. The second byway section runs from Jefferson to Laurel Springs on NC 88. At Laurel Springs, NC 88 meets NC 18 and the Blue Ridge Parkway crosses the community.

moments.title: Todd
moments.text: Todd grew beside the South Fork of the New River, first as the farming community of Elk Cross Roads. Timber harvesting and mica and copper mining brought growth in the later nineteenth century. The Virginia–Carolina Railway announced its extension to Elk Cross Roads in 1910. Its train earned the name Virginia Creeper for its slow climb up steep grades. By 1934, the timber was exhausted and the Depression forced rail service to end. A 1940 flood then washed away buildings. North Carolina revoked the town charter in the 1970s; cultural tourism and second-home communities brought renewed activity in the twenty-first century.

moments.title: West Jefferson
moments.text: West Jefferson owes its creation to the railroad, becoming a major stop and incorporating in 1909. Norfolk and Western served the town for decades. As rail service declined and textile jobs went overseas, the economy shifted increasingly toward tourism. Its historic district contains 50 contributing buildings, chiefly one- and two-story commercial structures from the early to middle twentieth century. Among them are the West Jefferson Depot and the Parkway Theater, built in 1939. Along the walkable main street are local art and a vintage theater; a caboose is also among the town's attractions.

moments.title: Laurel Springs
moments.text: NC 88 reaches Laurel Springs at its junction with NC 18, near the Ashe County line. The Blue Ridge Parkway crosses the center of this Alleghany County community. Here the Robert L. Doughton House dates to 1899: a two-story frame farmhouse with a steep hip roof and a projecting gable.
